title: Lamrim: death
hookLine: death is certain, its time uncertain, only practice helps at that time

lines: THE RIVER RISES IN THE NIGHT.
cards: A village asleep in a river valley. Lamps out, doors shut, everyone dreaming about tomorrow's chores. In the night the river rises, and by morning the village is gone.
The Dhammapada uses that picture for a person wrapped up in family and possessions, carried off by death before they've looked up. It's not a gentle image, and it isn't meant to be.
Yesterday the lamrim said this life is precious. Today it adds the other half, the one that gives the first its weight: this precious life will end, and nobody knows when.

teach.b: You met this on day six hundred three, in the dart of grief; here the lamrim makes it a stair. First, death is certain. The lamrim doesn't ask anyone to dwell on gloom, only to notice that no one who was born has stayed.
The great teachers died. The Buddha died. Every person in an old photograph is gone or going.
None of this is news, yet the mind lives as if it were someone else's news.
Second, the time is uncertain. A life has no fixed length.
Healthy people die suddenly, the old sometimes outlive the young, and the things that keep a body alive, food, a car, a doctor's medicine, can in a bad moment be the things that end it.
Tomorrow is not a promise; it's a likely guess.

teach.h: AT THAT TIME, ONLY PRACTICE HELPS.
teach.b: Third, at that time only practice helps. The Dhammapada says that when death seizes someone, sons are no help, nor a father, nor relatives. The lamrim adds wealth and the body itself.

What goes with you, in this teaching, is the shape your mind has taken: the patience, the kindness, the clarity you actually practiced. Fourth, why it belongs here. Precious life alone can turn into a reason to relax.
Precious life plus an unknown end turns into urgency, the good kind: not panic, but a clear sense of what matters today.
And if thoughts of death feel close or heavy today, you don't have to carry them alone: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

how: In lamrim practice, students meditate on death's certainty, the uncertainty of its time, and that only practice helps at death, reflecting on each point in turn during regular meditation sessions.

s: the lamrim's death meditation is meant to make you gloomy
it's meant to make urgency clear: not panic, but a sense of what matters today.
the Dhammapada says kin are no help when death seizes someone
it names sons, a father and relatives; the lamrim adds wealth and the body.
lamrim teaches death before precious human life
precious human life comes first; death follows and gives it urgency.

games.q: you've just sat with 'this life will end, and I don't know when'. a friend's call you've been putting off is on your list. what does the teaching point toward?
o: leave it for next week; there's plenty of time.
make the call today, since tomorrow is a guess.
games.why: certain and uncertain together sort what matters: the lamrim aims at clear urgency, not despair.

practice: Say quietly to yourself, this life will end, and let it sit for a few breaths; then, I don't know when. Ask gently, without pressure: if that's true, what matters today?
If this feels too heavy right now, simply rest with the breath instead.

wordCard.voice: Lamrim, the next stair: death. Certain that it comes, uncertain when, and at that time only practice helps. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: maranasati, mindfulness of death, the practice behind this stage.

carryVoice: Your line: certain, uncertain. Held together, they sort the important from the merely loud. See you tomorrow.
